decisions.0: Ace-three suited calls the hijack's open from the big blind: the price is cheap and a suited ace can make good pairs and the strongest hands of its suit. It 3-bets now and then; folding is the mistake.
decisions.1: Top pair with a three kicker is ahead of most of the hijack's small bets, which it makes with almost every hand, but any better ace beats you. Calling keeps the bluffs and weaker pairs in and the pot small; raising folds those and gets called by better aces. So calling is the natural play, and folding would be a big mistake.
decisions.2: The eight means your three kicker no longer plays; your top pair is now a medium-strength hand. Check: the hijack then bets about half the time, often with draws and bluffs you beat, while its weaker pairs like kings and jacks mostly check back. A bet from you would fold those weaker hands and get called by better aces, which is why betting three quarters of the pot costs 0.37 bb.
decisions.3: After the hijack checks back the turn, your top pair beats most of its range: kings, jacks, tens and queens that did not bet. A half-pot bet gets called by many of those; checking lets the hijack bluff or check behind. Both are about equally good, and the bet is a little more common. A bet bigger than the pot folds those weaker pairs and costs 0.32 bb.

takeaway: With top pair and a weak kicker, check when only better hands would call, and bet small once the weaker hands have shown up.
